title: Tree and a Turd
author: Josh Fisher
summary: Continuing a series on teaching fractions, the author works through how to extend students' intuitive grasp of halves to other fraction names using the template '___ are any of ___ equal parts of a whole,' combining a number line with a fraction-strip/tape-diagram overlay. He argues for letting students generalize fraction structure from representation and language rather than introducing it as a procedural 'count the parts' rule, to avoid a mismatch that causes later confusion.
points: Proposes a generalizable sentence template — '___ are any of ___ equal parts of a whole' — to extend halves-intuition to thirds, fourths, and beyond.
Warns against introducing fractions as 'number of equal parts, number of parts to count,' arguing students should discover that structure themselves through representation.
Combines a number line with a fraction-strip/tape-diagram overlay as a scaffold, while noting the combination may still carry cognitive load costs worth revisiting.
Frames the throughline of the unit as: fraction sizes shrink as denominators grow, a tension between grid density and phase alignment.
Flags remaining threads for later passes: reinforcing n/n = 1/1, introducing mixed numbers, and building in estimation practice.
quotes: In this part of the fraction story, we now extend our (measurement-unit) intuitions about wholes and halves to the rest of the fraction names
One reason for reiterating this sentence frame is that it is closer to how we talk about fractions.
The combination number-line and fraction strip(s)—or 'tape diagram' for all you keep-austin-weirdos—started as shorthand, but I like it.
The subtext throughout is that fraction sizes get smaller as denominators (going down on the page; important now and later) get bigger
Other mentionables: n/n = 1/1 is reinforced over and over, mixed numbers quickly, just to get out the construction for now, and estimation!
